tips.title: Series shares pd, parallel shares current
tips.body: In **series** the **current is the same** everywhere and the **pd is shared**. In **parallel** the **pd is the same** across each branch and the **current is shared**. Learn them as a mirror pair and neither can be forgotten.

tips.title: Only series resistances add
tips.body: **$R_{total} = R_1 + R_2$ applies to series only.** In parallel the total is **less than the smallest** individual resistor — and the specification says you are **not required to calculate it**, only to know that it falls.

tips.title: The bigger resistor takes the bigger share
tips.body: In a series circuit the pd splits **in proportion to resistance**. With 4 Ω and 8 Ω across 12 V, the pds are 4 V and 8 V. If your two pds do not add back to the supply, something is wrong.

tips.title: Parallel adds a route, not an obstacle
tips.body: Adding a resistor in **parallel** gives the current **another path**, so more current flows in total and the **total resistance falls**. Adding one in **series** puts it **in the way**, so the total rises. Thinking in paths makes the rule obvious.

tips.title: Check your answer adds up
tips.body: Series: the **pds must sum to the supply**. Parallel: the **branch currents must sum to the total**. Both are free checks that catch nearly every arithmetic slip in this topic.

why.matters:
Any circuit, however tangled, is series pieces and parallel pieces, and each kind obeys three rules. Reducing a wiring diagram to one equivalent resistance is what lets you say what current a supply will have to give, whether a fuse will hold, and why a meter must go where it goes.

Every fault an electrician finds and every circuit question in the exam is the same six rules, applied from the inside out.

examples.title: Why an ammeter must never go across the battery
examples.body:
The two meters are opposites, and the rules say why. A **voltmeter** measures pd, so it goes across a component, and to leave the circuit alone it has a very high resistance. An **ammeter** measures current, so it goes in the path, and to leave the circuit alone it has a very low resistance.

That low resistance is the trap. Put an ammeter across a supply, as if it were a voltmeter, and it is a near-short circuit: $I = V \div R$ with a tiny $R$ gives a huge current, and the meter's fuse blows. A voltmeter in series just stops the circuit.

props.title: Two meters, two resistances, two mistakes

visual.alt: A table contrasting an ammeter, with very low resistance, which reads current in series and short-circuits a supply if put across it, with a voltmeter, with very high resistance, which reads pd across a component and stops the circuit if put in series

examples.title: The lines on the rear window
examples.body:
The demister on a car's back window is a set of thin heating strips, and every strip is its own branch across the 12 V battery: **parallel**. With, say, 3 strips of 12 Ω, each has the full 12 V across it and draws $12 \div 12 = 1$ A, so the battery supplies 3 A.

Scratch one strip through and only that branch goes cold; the others keep their 12 V and their 1 A, and the battery supplies 2 A. Wired in series, one scratch would kill the whole window. The parallel grid also has a lower resistance than any one strip, 4 Ω here.

visual.alt: A parallel circuit of three twelve ohm heating strips across a twelve volt car battery, each with the full twelve volts and one amp, the currents adding to three amps

examples.title: Why an amplifier says "minimum 4 Ω"
examples.body:
A speaker is printed with its resistance, usually 8 Ω, and the back of an amplifier says the least it will drive, often *4 Ω*. Those two numbers are the parallel rule.

Plug a second 8 Ω speaker into the same output and the pair are in parallel: total resistance $8 \div 2 = 4$ Ω, less than either, so the amplifier has to supply **twice** the current for the same pd. A third takes it to 2.7 Ω and three times the current. The amplifier's output transistors are built for a certain current, and past it they overheat. *Minimum 4 Ω* means *two speakers, not three*.

visual.alt: A table showing one, two and three eight ohm speakers in parallel giving eight, four and about two point seven ohms, so the amplifier supplies one, two and three times the current

steps.title: The two ways of joining components
steps.body:
**There are two ways of joining electrical components: in series and in parallel.** Some circuits include both.

**Series** means components are joined **one after another** in a single loop, so there is only **one path** for the current.

**Parallel** means components are joined **side by side**, each on its own **branch**, so the current has **more than one path**.

**For components connected in series**, the specification gives three rules:

- there is the **same current** through each component
- the **total potential difference of the supply is shared** between the components
- the **total resistance** of two components is the **sum** of each: $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2$

**For components connected in parallel**, three mirror-image rules:

- the **potential difference across each component is the same**
- the **total current** through the whole circuit is the **sum** of the currents through the separate components
- the **total resistance of two resistors is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor**

**Notice the symmetry.** Series shares **potential difference** and keeps current the same; parallel shares **current** and keeps potential difference the same. Learning them as a pair is far more reliable than learning six separate facts.

check.prompt: In a series circuit, what is true of the current?
options: It is shared between the components
It is the same through every component
It is largest through the biggest resistor
It is different in each part of the circuit
check.solution: In **series** there is **one path**, so the **same current** flows through every component. It is the **potential difference** that is shared.

steps.title: Why the totals move as they do
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to explain qualitatively why adding resistors in series increases the total resistance, whilst adding resistors in parallel decreases it.** Thinking in **paths** makes both obvious.

**Adding in series puts another obstacle in the way.** There is still only **one path**, and the current must now pass through **more** resistance, so the total rises and the current falls. With 4 Ω and 8 Ω in series the total is $4 + 8 = 12$ Ω.

**Adding in parallel gives the current another route.** Each new branch is an **extra path** the charge can take, so **more current flows in total** for the same potential difference. Since $R = V \div I$, a larger total current with the same pd means a **smaller total resistance**.

**A useful picture.** Series is adding another narrow corridor to the end of the corridor you are already in — harder to get through. Parallel is opening a second door into the same room — easier.

**That is why the parallel total is below the smallest resistor.** Whatever current the smallest resistor was carrying on its own, it still carries — and the other branches add **more** on top. More total current at the same pd must mean less total resistance than that branch alone had.

**The specification is explicit that you are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel.** You must know that it **falls below the smallest**, and why, but the reciprocal formula is not needed.

steps.title: Working out a series circuit
steps.body: **The specification asks you to calculate the currents, potential differences and resistances in dc series circuits**, and to solve problems using the idea of equivalent resistance.

visuals.problem: A 12 V supply is connected in series to a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. Find the total resistance, the current, and the pd across each resistor.

steps.text: **Total resistance** first: in series the resistances add. $R = 4 + 8 = $ **12 Ω**
steps.note: this "equivalent resistance" lets you treat the pair as a single resistor

steps.text: **Current** next, using the supply pd and the total resistance: $I = V \div R = 12 \div 12 = $ **1 A**
steps.note: use the TOTAL resistance here, not one of the individual ones

steps.text: In series the **current is the same everywhere**, so **1 A** flows through both resistors
steps.note: this is the step that makes the rest possible — one current, used twice

steps.text: **pd across the 4 Ω resistor**: $V = I R = 1 \times 4 = $ **4 V**
steps.note: now use the individual resistance, with the current you just found
the larger resistance takes the larger share of the potential difference
the shared pds must add back to the supply — a free check that catches almost every slip

props.title: Total resistance, then current, then each pd — always in that order

visuals.alt: A table working through a series circuit step by step from total resistance to the check

check.prompt: A 12 V supply is in series with a 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor. What is the current, in amperes?
check.solution: Total resistance $= 4 + 8 = 12$ Ω. Then $I = V \div R = 12 \div 12 = $ **1 A**.

steps.title: Working out a parallel circuit
steps.body:
**In parallel the reasoning runs the other way**, because it is now the **potential difference** that is shared out to everything equally.

**Each branch gets the full supply pd.** With the same 12 V supply across a 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor in **parallel**, **both** have the **full 12 V** across them.

**So each branch current is found separately**, using that branch's own resistance:

- through the 4 Ω branch: $I = 12 \div 4 = $ **3 A**
- through the 8 Ω branch: $I = 12 \div 8 = $ **1.5 A**

**The total current is the sum**: $3 + 1.5 = $ **4.5 A**.

**Compare that with the series version.** The same two resistors across the same supply gave **1 A** in series but **4.5 A** in parallel — more than four times as much. The components have not changed; only the wiring has.

**And notice what that tells you about the total resistance.** The 4 Ω branch alone would carry 3 A. Together the pair carries **more** than that, at the same pd — so the total resistance must be **less than 4 Ω**, the smaller of the two. That is the rule, arrived at without any formula.

**Why homes are wired in parallel.** Each appliance gets the **full mains pd**, and each can be **switched off independently** without breaking the others' circuit. In series, switching off one would stop them all.

check.prompt: A 12 V supply is across a 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor in parallel. What is the total current, in amperes?
check.solution: Each branch has the full 12 V. $12 \div 4 = 3$ A and $12 \div 8 = 1.5$ A. The total is $3 + 1.5 = $ **4.5 A**.

steps.title: Measuring, and circuit diagrams
steps.body:
**Meters go in different places because they measure different things.**

**An ammeter measures the current through a component**, so it must be in the path — **connected in series**. It has a very low resistance, so adding it changes the circuit as little as possible.

**A voltmeter measures the potential difference across a component**, so it goes **in parallel** with that component, bridging across it. It has a very high resistance, so almost no current is diverted through it.

**A memory hook**: *through* → in series; *across* → in parallel. The preposition tells you the connection.

**Using dc series circuits for measurement and testing.** The specification asks you to explain the design and use of dc series circuits for this purpose. A series circuit is useful for testing because there is **one current** to measure, and it passes through **every** component — so a single ammeter reading applies to the whole loop. Placing a component in series with a known resistor and reading the pd across each lets you work out the unknown resistance.

**Circuit diagrams.** You should be able to use them to construct and check both kinds of circuit. When reading one, trace the path from one terminal of the supply to the other: if there is only **one** route, it is series; if the path **splits and rejoins**, those parts are parallel.

**Many real circuits are both.** A pair of resistors in parallel might sit in series with a third. Deal with such a circuit in **parts**: work out each section on its own rules before combining.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Learn the two sets of rules as mirror images.** Series: **same current**, **shared pd**, resistances **add**. Parallel: **same pd**, **shared current**, total resistance **below the smallest**. Six facts become two patterns.

**Use the total resistance to find the current.** In a series circuit, $I = V_{supply} \div R_{total}$. Dividing the supply pd by just one of the resistors is the commonest error, and it gives a current that is far too large.

**Then use each individual resistance for each pd.** One current, applied twice with different resistances. Keeping straight which resistance belongs to which step is what the calculation is really testing.

**Always check the sums.** In series the **pds must add to the supply**; in parallel the **branch currents must add to the total**. These are free checks and they catch nearly everything.

**Explain the resistance rules by paths, not by formula.** Series adds **another obstacle in the one path**, so resistance rises. Parallel adds **another route**, so more current flows at the same pd and the total resistance falls. The specification asks for this **qualitatively**, so the reasoning is the answer.

**Know what you are not asked to do.** The specification states plainly that students are **not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel**. Know that it falls **below the smallest**, and why. Time spent on the reciprocal formula is time not spent on what is examined.

**Justify the parallel rule without a formula.** The smallest branch alone carries a certain current; adding branches means the pair carries **more** at the **same** pd, so by $R = V \div I$ the total resistance must be **smaller than that branch had alone**. That argument earns full marks and needs no algebra.

**Explain meter resistances.** An **ammeter** has **very low** resistance so that inserting it does not reduce the current it is trying to measure. A **voltmeter** has **very high** resistance so that almost no current is diverted down it. Both are examples of an instrument being designed not to disturb what it measures.

**Give the real reason houses are wired in parallel**: each appliance receives the **full mains pd**, and each can be **switched independently** without breaking the others' circuit.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Series**: one path. **Parallel**: more than one path.
- **Series**: the **same current** through each component.
- **Series**: the supply pd is **shared** between components.
- **Series**: $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2$.
- **Parallel**: the **pd across each component is the same**.
- **Parallel**: the **total current is the sum** of the branch currents.
- **Parallel**: the total resistance is **less than the smallest** resistor.
- You are **not required to calculate** the parallel total.
- Adding in **series** adds an **obstacle** → resistance **rises**.
- Adding in **parallel** adds a **path** → resistance **falls**.
- Find the series current from the **total** resistance: $I = V \div R_{total}$.
- The **larger** resistance takes the **larger share** of the pd.
- **Check**: series pds add to the supply; parallel currents add to the total.
- **Ammeter** in **series**, very **low** resistance. **Voltmeter** in **parallel**, very **high** resistance.
- Houses are wired in **parallel**: full pd to each appliance, and independent switching.

questions.prompt: Compare series and parallel circuits, explaining the rules for current, potential difference and resistance, and why the total resistance changes as it does.
questions.solution:
There are two ways of joining components, and the rules for them mirror one another.

**In series** the components are joined one after another, so there is only **one path** for the current. This gives three rules. First, there is the **same current through each component**, because every charge must pass through all of them in turn. Second, the **total potential difference of the supply is shared** between the components. Third, the **total resistance is the sum** of the individual resistances: $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2$.

**In parallel** the components are on separate branches, so the current has **more than one path**. The rules mirror the series ones. The **potential difference across each component is the same**, because each branch is connected directly across the supply. The **total current is the sum of the branch currents**. And the **total resistance of two resistors is less than the smallest individual resistor**.

So series shares the **potential difference** and keeps the current common; parallel shares the **current** and keeps the potential difference common.

**Why the totals move in opposite directions** is best explained by thinking about **paths**.

Adding a resistor **in series** puts **another obstacle into the single path**. The current has no alternative route, and must now push through more resistance than before, so the **total resistance rises** and the current falls.

Adding a resistor **in parallel** gives the current an **extra route**. The existing branches still carry exactly the current they carried before, because the potential difference across them has not changed — and the new branch carries **more** current on top of that. So the **total current increases** while the potential difference stays the same, and since $R = V \div I$, a larger current at the same pd means a **smaller total resistance**.

That argument also explains why the parallel total must fall **below the smallest** resistor. Whatever current the smallest branch carried alone, the combination carries **more** than that at the same pd — so the combination must have **less** resistance than that branch had by itself.

A worked comparison makes the difference concrete. A 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor across a 12 V supply give a total of 12 Ω and a current of **1 A** in series. Wired in parallel, the branches carry 3 A and 1.5 A, a total of **4.5 A** — over four times as much, from the same components and the same supply. Only the wiring changed.

It is worth noting that the specification does **not** require the total resistance of two parallel resistors to be calculated — only that you know it falls below the smallest, and why.

questions.prompt: A 12 V supply is connected in series to a 4 Ω and an 8 Ω resistor. Calculate the current and the potential difference across each resistor, explaining each step, and describe how you would check your answers.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the total resistance.** The resistors are in series, so their resistances add:

$$R_{total} = 4 + 8 = \mathbf{12\ \Omega}$$

This is the **equivalent resistance**: the whole circuit now behaves exactly as a single 12 Ω resistor would.

**Step 2 — the current.** Using $V = IR$ rearranged, with the **supply** potential difference and the **total** resistance:

$$I = \frac{V}{R_{total}} = \frac{12}{12} = \mathbf{1\ A}$$

It is essential to use the **total** resistance here. Dividing 12 V by just the 4 Ω resistor would give 3 A, which is three times too large, because the current is opposed by **everything** in the single path — not by one component at a time.

**Step 3 — the current through each resistor.** In a series circuit there is only **one path**, so the **same current flows through every component**. Both resistors therefore carry **1 A**. This is the step that makes the rest possible: one current, used twice.

**Step 4 — the potential difference across each.** Now apply $V = IR$ to each resistor separately, using the **individual** resistance and the current just found:

Across the 4 Ω resistor: $V = 1 \times 4 = \mathbf{4\ V}$

Across the 8 Ω resistor: $V = 1 \times 8 = \mathbf{8\ V}$

Notice that the **larger resistance takes the larger share** of the potential difference. That follows directly from $V = IR$ with a common current: the pd divides in **proportion to the resistance**. The 8 Ω resistor has twice the resistance, so it takes twice the pd.

**How to check.** The strongest check is that in a series circuit the **potential differences across the components must add up to the supply potential difference**, since the supply pd is shared between them:

$$4 + 8 = 12\ \text{V} \quad \checkmark$$

This matches the 12 V supply, so the answers are consistent. The check is free, takes seconds, and catches almost every arithmetic or rearrangement slip in a series calculation — if the pds had come to 10 V or 16 V, there would be a mistake to find.

A second check is on **plausibility**: 1 A through 12 Ω requires 12 V, which is what the supply provides. A third would be to verify with power: $P = VI = 12 \times 1 = 12$ W for the whole circuit, and $4 \times 1 + 8 \times 1 = 12$ W across the two resistors — the energy transferred in the components accounts for all the energy supplied.

examTechnique.body:
Learn the rules as **mirror images**: series shares **pd** and keeps current common; parallel shares **current** and keeps pd common. Only **series** resistances add.

Find the series current from the **total** resistance, then use each **individual** resistance for each pd. **Check**: series pds add to the supply, parallel currents add to the total.
examinerErrors: Dividing the supply pd by one resistor instead of the total.
Applying the series rules to a parallel circuit, or the reverse.
Adding resistances for a parallel combination.
Saying the parallel total lies between the two resistances.
Reaching for the reciprocal formula, which is not required.
Connecting an ammeter in parallel or a voltmeter in series.
Explaining parallel resistance with no mention of extra paths.
Never checking that the pds add back to the supply.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the two rule sets as **mirror images** rather than six separate facts, and finds the series current from the **total** resistance before using each **individual** resistance for each pd. It explains the resistance rules by **paths** — series adds an obstacle, parallel adds a route — and can justify that the parallel total falls **below the smallest** without any formula, by noting the pair carries more current than the smallest branch did alone at the same pd. It knows the reciprocal formula is **not required**, explains why an ammeter has **low** and a voltmeter **high** resistance, and always **checks** that the pds add back to the supply.
